sentences.text: Saurornitholestes was a small, bipedal carnivorous dinosaur equipped with a sickle-shaped retractable claw on the second toe of each foot.
The type species Saurornitholestes langstoni measured between 1.3 and 1.8 meters long and weighed between 5 and 22.5 kilograms.
Some estimates place the length at approximately 1.8 meters and the weight at about 10 kilograms.
Fossils representing neonate-sized individuals of Saurornitholestes have been reported.
The genus Saurornitholestes was described by Hans-Dieter Sues in 1978.
This description was published by Sues in 1978.
Two species of Saurornitholestes have been named: Saurornitholestes langstoni in 1978 and Saurornitholestes sullivani in 2015.
A species formerly assigned to the genus, Saurornitholestes robustus, was described by Sullivan in 2006, though it is now believed to deserve its own genus.
Robert Sullivan named the species Saurornitholestes robustus in 2006 based on a left frontal bone.
The holotype skeleton of Saurornitholestes was discovered in 1974 by amateur paleontologist Irene Vanderloh near Steveville, Alberta.
A Canadian amateur paleontologist named Irene Vanderloh discovered a small theropod skeleton near Steveville, Alberta, in 1974.
Aase Roland Jacobsen described a dentary of Saurornitholestes in 2001.
The described dentary is about 12 centimeters long and preserves fifteen tooth positions, ten of which retain teeth.
Saurornitholestes sullivani likely had a keen sense of smell, indicated by an unusually large olfactory bulb in its skull.
Researchers suggest that the second premaxillary teeth of Saurornitholestes may have been specialized for preening feathers.
The feeding habits of Saurornitholestes were typical of ceratosaurian theropods, using a characteristic stab and throw feeding method.
Microwear on the teeth indicated that Saurornitholestes likely preferred larger prey than the troodontids sharing its environment.
Teeth of Saurornitholestes have been found embedded in the wing bone of the pterosaur Quetzalcoatlus.
Because the pterosaur was much larger than Saurornitholestes, Currie and Jacobsen suggest the theropod fed on the carcass of this animal.

Saurornitholestes appears to have been the most common small theropod in Dinosaur Provincial Park, with its teeth and bones being much more common than those of its massive contemporary, Dromaeosaurus.
Two of the nine examined Saurornitholestes hand bones were found to have stress fractures.
Three toothmarks were visible on the inner surface of a Saurornitholestes dentary.
While the specific maker cannot be identified, the most likely perpetrator of the toothmarks is hypothesized to be a juvenile tyrannosaurid like Gorgosaurus or Daspletosaurus.
The striations causing the marks are between 0.37 and 0.40 millimeters thick with cuboidal cross-sections.
Hans-Dieter Sues originally assigned Saurornitholestes to the family Dromaeosauridae in 1978.
In 1978, Sues assigned Saurornitholestes to Dromaeosauridae.
A 2019 analysis by Philip J. Currie and David C. Evans recovered Saurornitholestes as the sister taxon to Atrociraptor.
Saurornitholestes lived during the late Cretaceous period, approximately between 77 and 68 million years ago, from the Campanian to Maastrichtian stages, in what is now North America.
Fossils attributed to Saurornitholestes langstoni have been found in the Oldman Formation dating to about 77 million years ago and the Dos Medicinas Formation dating to about 72 million years ago.
Saurornitholestes fossils have been found on both sides of the Western Interior Seaway.
Saurornitholestes was found on both sides of the Western Interior Seaway.
Fossils of Saurornitholestes date to the Late Cretaceous, with possible records extending to the Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary.
It is debated whether Saurornitholestes robustus is a valid dromaeosaurid, an indeterminate theropod, or a troodontid.
G. S. Paul concluded that Saurornitholestes is a more modern synonym of Velociraptor, though this is debated.

A later phylogenetic overview claimed S. robustus lacked dromaeosaurid characters and should be considered an indeterminate theropod, while a 2014 study went further to demonstrate it could be assigned to Troodontidae based on similarities with troodontids.
